title: The Elohim plural and the canonical gloss
statement: The Hebrew word Elohim is grammatically plural and the biblical text preserves plural usage around it (plural cohortatives, plural pronouns, the sons-of-God formulae, the divine council of Psalm 82); the corpus reads that plurality referentially — many individual Elohim rather than a majestic singular — and adopts the canon's gloss 'those who came from the sky', while recording explicitly that the gloss is a canonical rendering and not the consensus lexical derivation.

includes: The philological layer, which is mainstream and direct: Elohim is morphologically plural (plural of Eloah); Genesis 1:26 ('let us make') and 3:22 ('as one of us') preserve plural forms; benei ha-elohim and the Psalm 82 assembly preserve plural divine beings
The referential reading, which is framework: the plural forms are read as referring to a plurality of individual beings, against the conventional plural-of-majesty resolution

The canonical gloss, which is canon-explicit and labelled: 'those who came from the sky' is the canon's rendering; the record states plainly that this is not the consensus etymology (which derives Elohim through Eloah/El)
The translation-history observation: the singular-God rendering is a translation decision with a history, not a property of the Hebrew text
excludes: Any claim that the plural morphology alone proves plural referents; morphological form does not yield full syntactic meaning without contextual analysis (an invalid transition the claim model names)
Any claim that the canonical gloss is philologically derived; it is recorded as canonical, full stop
Uniformity of reference across all biblical uses of elohim; the term's reference varies by passage and period
The historicity of the beings referred to, which is woh-claim-0001's burden, not this record's

source_references.locator: Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (Elohim/Eloha, the singular-God translation, and its consequences); the gloss 'those who came from the sky' throughout the opening narrative
GEN-WOH-1:26 (na'aseh, plural cohortative); GEN-WOH-3:22 ('as one of us'); GEN-WOH-6:2 (benei ha-elohim)
PSA-82:1 (elohim standing in the assembly of El, judging among elohim); 82:6-7 (the sentence on the assembly)
Mark S. Smith's treatment of Israelite divine plurality and the development toward monotheism — the mainstream account the referential reading engages
The academic account of the Raelian reinterpretation of Elohim, including the philological objections to it

alternatives.statement: The plural morphology with singular verbs is a plural of majesty or abstraction, a known Hebrew construction; no plural referent follows.
The plural passages address a heavenly court subordinate to a single God — plurality of beings without plurality of gods, the standard scholarly reading of Psalm 82 and Genesis 1:26.
The plural traces are fossils of an earlier polytheism edited toward monotheism; they testify to religion's development, not to remembered beings.
The consensus derivation of Elohim through Eloah/El is correct and complete; the canonical gloss has no philological standing.

revision_triggers: Source-language review materially changes any of the cited plural-usage observations.
Public prose begins presenting the canonical gloss as an etymology, which this record excludes and the epistemic principles forbid.
Claim woh-claim-0001 is revised or retired.
The referential reading fails to engage a new consensus treatment of the divine-council material.
